report:
## Conclusion

Yes, the evidence indicates that masks can reduce COVID-19 infections when worn by a large proportion of the population. Multiple studies and systematic reviews support this finding:

- A **2025 systematic review** published in MDPI concluded that "masking policies and mask wearing are beneficial to prevent and reduce the risk of SARS-CoV-2 infections and COVID-19 disease in various real-world settings." ([MDPI, 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/1660-4601/22/10/1590))

- A **PNAS study (2022)** that directly measured mask wearing (rather than just mandates) found that population mask wearing notably reduced SARS-CoV-2 transmission, with mean mask-wearing levels corresponding to a **19% decrease** in transmission. ([PNAS, 2022](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2119266119))

- A landmark **randomized controlled trial in Bangladesh** (discussed in The Conversation) found that promoting mask use in villages reduced COVID-19-like symptoms by **12%** overall, with a **35% reduction** among people aged 60+ and **23%** among those aged 50–60. Surgical masks outperformed cloth masks. ([The Conversation](https://theconversation.com/evidence-shows-that-yes-masks-prevent-covid-19-and-surgical-masks-are-the-way-to-go-167963))

- A **2024 Cambridge review** assessed the full body of evidence, including the updated Cochrane review, and provided an unbiased assessment confirming that masking has a role in reducing respiratory viral transmission. ([Cambridge University Press, 2024](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/antimicrobial-stewardship-and-healthcare-epidemiology/article/masking-for-covid19-and-other-respiratory-viral-infections-implications-of-the-available-evidence/0B48A9D3AFD896E59E06CBBDDB056936))

**In summary:** The weight of evidence—from RCTs, observational studies, and systematic reviews—supports that widespread community mask wearing reduces SARS-CoV-2 transmission, with greater benefits for higher-quality masks (surgical/N95) and among older or more vulnerable populations. Effect sizes are moderate rather than absolute, but meaningful at the population level.
